title: Skin surgery procedures: excision, curettage, cryotherapy & Mohs
summary: What each procedure is for, at knowledge level: elliptical excision along relaxed skin tension lines, shave and punch biopsy, curettage and cautery, cryotherapy (and its blisters), Mohs surgery, flaps and grafts.

glance.think: Explaining a planned procedure to a patient, or recognising expected after-effects (cryotherapy blisters, flap scars).
glance.engine: Each technique trades tissue sampling, margin control, cosmesis and recurrence differently.
glance.backbone: Excision for diagnosis and most cancers (3:1 ellipse along RSTLs); C&C for small low-risk lesions; cryotherapy only for confidently diagnosed benign or low-risk lesions; Mohs for high-risk or recurrent facial BCC.
glance.never_miss: Freezing an undiagnosed lesion (no histology, recurrence); cryotherapy blisters and pigment loss in skin of colour.

what: **Concepts only, for understanding referrals, consent and aftercare. Performing these needs supervised training and credentialing.**

rows: **Shave excision/biopsy**
Removes a raised lesion level with the skin
SK, dermal naevus (cosmetic, private), skin tags, some BCC biopsies
Yes
**Not for suspected melanoma** (Breslow lost); naevi may recur
**Curettage & cautery (C&C)**
Scrapes off friable tissue, then cauterises the base
**Pyogenic granuloma**, SK, small low-risk BCC (trunk/limbs), viral warts
Yes (fragmented)
No margin assessment. Not for high-risk or facial BCC or for melanoma
**Punch biopsy**
Cylindrical core (2–8 mm)
Diagnosing rashes and tumours (BCC/SCC subtype, MF)
Yes
Samples only part; **not for melanoma diagnosis** (except specialist situations)
**Elliptical excision**
Full-thickness removal with margin, closed in a line
Suspected malignancy (with margin), symptomatic benign lesions, cysts
Yes (with margins)
Scar about 3× the lesion length; oriented along **relaxed skin tension lines (RSTL)**
**Cryotherapy**
Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C) freezes and destroys tissue
**AK, viral warts, SK**, some superficial BCC (specialist)
**Never on an undiagnosed or pigmented lesion that might be melanoma**
**Electrosurgery**
Heat or current: electrocautery (heated wire, no current through the patient), electrodesiccation/fulguration, electrosection, **bipolar diathermy** (current between forceps tips)
Haemostasis, C&C, small lesions
Variable
Pacemakers/ICDs (see *Antibiotic prophylaxis and cardiac devices*); burns; fire risk with alcohol prep (see *Room, PPE, skin preparation, specimen handling and the fail-safe*); smoke plume
**Secondary intention**
Leaves the wound to heal by granulation
**Concave sites** (inner canthus, nasal alar groove, conchal bowl, temple), after C&C or shave, Mohs defects
Slower (weeks); dressing burden; contraction near free margins
**Undermining**
Freeing the skin edges in a tissue plane to reduce tension before closure
Larger ellipses
Haematoma risk; danger zones
**Flaps / grafts**
Moving adjacent skin (flap) or transferring skin from elsewhere (graft) to close defects
Larger facial defects after cancer excision
Specialist
**Mohs micrographic surgery**
Staged excision with **complete (100%) peripheral and deep margin examination** on frozen sections, repeated until clear
High-risk/recurrent BCC (BAD 2021), some cSCC, DFSP, LM (specialist)
Yes
Specialist centres; time-consuming

list: **Langer's lines** were mapped on cadavers (collagen orientation). Surgeons now prefer **relaxed skin tension lines (RSTL)** (Borges), seen as natural wrinkle lines in a living person and found by pinching the skin.

Placing scars **parallel to RSTL** gives narrower, less visible scars. In practice: horizontal on the forehead, radial around the mouth and eyes, transverse in the neck creases, and along the long axis of limbs for melanoma excision biopsies (lymphatic drainage).
**Expected reactions:** redness and swelling within hours; **blister** (sometimes **haemorrhagic**) within 24–48 h; periorbital oedema after facial treatment; crusting and healing over 1–3 weeks

**Adverse effects:** **hypopigmentation** (avoid or use caution in skin of colour); hyperpigmentation; scarring; nail dystrophy; **nerve damage** over superficial nerves (sides of fingers); tendon damage; **recurrence or missed cancer** (recurrent BCC after cryotherapy)
**Cautions:** cold urticaria, cryoglobulinaemia, Raynaud's, poor circulation (lower legs in elderly people heal poorly), and **undiagnosed lesions**.

**NHS:** commissioning for warts and SK is restricted in many areas (EBI/local policies). Self-care alternatives for warts: salicylic acid, OTC cryogen products (dimethyl ether/propane). These are less effective but suitable for many patients.

A **friable, bleeding vascular lesion** that would bleed during shave alone. **C&C removes it and seals the base**, and the curettings go for **histology** (amelanotic melanoma, SCC and Kaposi are the "must-not-miss" mimics; the [skin lumps](condition:dermatofibroma) notes see *Procedures at knowledge level*).

Alternatives: shave + cautery; excision for recurrent lesions (with closure, as course teaching described); silver nitrate or cryotherapy for very small lesions where the diagnosis is certain (no specimen).
**Posterior neck:** superficial procedures are safe. A deeper excision would need awareness of the spinal accessory nerve (see *Consent, complications and anatomical danger zones*).
surgery (standard excision 4 mm / ≥5 mm margins) → Mohs for high-risk/recurrent
C&C or cryo for small low-risk lesions
imiquimod, 5-FU or PDT for superficial BCC

management: Use the table to explain to patients **why** a clinician chose a method, and why some lesions (suspected melanoma) must be excised whole by the specialist team rather than shaved or frozen.
red_flags: Never use cryotherapy on a lesion without a **confident diagnosis**: there is no histology and cancers can recur beneath the scar.
pearls: After cryotherapy: **leave blisters intact**, or drain with a sterile needle if tense and painful, keeping the roof. Use simple dressings and paracetamol. Seek help for signs of infection.
After C&C or shave: the wound is moist and heals over 2–3 weeks; petrolatum and a simple dressing.
